title: Spiral galaxy NGC 1232
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1232, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: NGC 1232 · constellation Eridanus · about 60 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #23 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Older, reddish stars fill the centre of this large spiral galaxy, while its arms are crowded with young blue stars and many regions where new stars are forming. This is NGC 1232, about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Eridanus, the River, photographed with ESO's Very Large Telescope and its FORS instrument.

Colour works as a rough clock for stars. The hottest, most massive stars shine blue but live only briefly, so blue light tends to mark places where stars formed recently. Older populations, which have lost their brightest members, glow redder, and that is why the core looks warmer in tone than the arms.

On the left side sits a distorted companion galaxy shaped like the Greek letter theta. Despite the great distance, the telescope's optical quality reveals a wealth of detail. The edge of the field corresponds to about 200,000 light-years, roughly twice the size of the Milky Way.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.78 x 6.83 arcminutes) and distance (60 million light years), the frame spans roughly 118,000 × 119,000 light-years. Its light set out about 60 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: ESO's Very Large Telescope with the FORS1 instrument made this from exposures in ultraviolet, blue and red light. The precise colour mapping for each filter isn't published.
filters: 420 nm · Optical B (Very Large Telescope FORS1)
360 nm · Ultraviolet U (Very Large Telescope FORS1)
600 nm · Optical R (Very Large Telescope FORS1)
understand.eye: Ultraviolet light is invisible to the eye, and the camera's exposures gathered far more light than an eye could, revealing faint detail in the arms.

explore: The picture combines three exposures taken through ultraviolet, blue and red filters during a spell of good observing conditions, with north at the top. NGC 1232 lies 20 degrees south of the celestial equator.
alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with a reddish centre and blue spiral arms, with a small distorted companion galaxy on the left.
